name: Telegraph cryptic crossword, All New book 4 No 51

book.title: The Telegraph All New Cryptic Crosswords 4

clue.text: A man going round the street lost?

indicators.note: something going round another thing encircles it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: taken as written
Ray is a man's name
St is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A man wandering round the street, wondering whether he has lost his way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A man' is read as one unit that wraps the street, a common way to split a two-word phrase around another piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To go astray is to wander off the right path, so astray describes someone or something that is lost.

clue.text: American city stream crossed by a dictator

indicators.note: a river crossed by something has that thing spanning it, read as one piece wrapped round the other

blocks.note: taken as written
Mao Zedong ruled China as a dictator
a rill is a small stream

explanation.surface: A river in a US city being crossed by a tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: The dictator is the Chinese leader Chairman Mao; his name straddles the little stream like a bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Amarillo is a city in the Texas Panhandle, so it is one example of an American city.

clue.text: Savalas — what did he appear on?

blocks.note: first meaning: the first name of the actor surnamed Savalas
second meaning: the British informal word for television, where he starred as Kojak

explanation.walkthrough: Telly Savalas played the TV detective Kojak; his first name is also British slang for television.
explanation.definitionFit: The actor's first name doubles as the informal British word for the television set his show was broadcast on.

clue.text: Denier of God? In death 'e is terrified!

indicators.note: 'in' says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: the letters run across death 'e is t

explanation.surface: A godless man faced with death is terrified, in a dropped-aitch voice.
explanation.definitionFit: An atheist rejects belief in any god, so the person denies God's existence.

clue.text: Professional educationist is investigated

blocks.note: pro is short for professional
a BEd, Bachelor of Education, is the degree a trained teacher holds

explanation.surface: A career teacher is the subject of an inquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: BEd is the British teaching degree, so an educationist is someone with a BEd.
explanation.definitionFit: To probe is to examine closely, so probed is a past-tense synonym for investigated.

clue.text: The price not hard to work out — from this bit of paper?

indicators.note: 'not' tells the solver to leave the following letter out
working something out rearranges it, so the remaining letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: The cost is easy to check from the slip of paper you were handed.
explanation.definitionFit: A receipt is the slip given when you pay, recording the price, so it is the bit of paper in question.

clue.text: Brother and I get vehicle — vehicle turning up with odds and ends

indicators.note: in a down answer, turning up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: Br is the abbreviation for brother
taken as written
a cab is a taxi
a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: Two siblings acquire a car, then another turns up full of junk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is just a joiner; the second vehicle is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Bric-a-brac means small miscellaneous ornaments and trinkets, which is what odds and ends are.

clue.text: Depression shown by duke in front of the fireplace …

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for duke
an ingle is a fireplace, as in inglenook

explanation.surface: A duke gloomily slumped before the hearth, his low mood leading into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in front of' just places the duke first. Depression here is a dip in the land, not a mood.
explanation.definitionFit: A dingle is a deep wooded hollow or dell, a natural depression in the ground.

clue.text: Maiden is unwell, with a temperature — falls on the doormat maybe

blocks.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
ails means is unwell
running a temperature makes one hot

explanation.surface: A young woman, sick and feverish, collapses onto the doormat.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture of someone fainting on the doormat hides the real reading: something delivered through the letterbox lands there.
explanation.definitionFit: A mailshot is a batch of advertising post sent out at once, the kind of thing that drops onto a doormat.

clue.text: …Time he had early drinks for depressed condition

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
taken as written
the contraction 'd stands for had, as in he'd
early in the sense of olden times
rums are drinks

explanation.surface: Continuing the duke's story: once he had drunk early in the day, he became gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this to the duke clue above for the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the doldrums means being stuck in low spirits, an idiom from the calm zone where sailing ships stalled.

clue.text: Piles of stones in Australian city

blocks.note: first meaning: heaps of stones built as landmarks or memorials
second meaning: a city in north Queensland

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests rubble somewhere in Australia; the two halves are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A cairn is a mound of stones used as a marker, and Cairns is a tropical Queensland city named after a governor.

clue.text: Woman of 51 left with little yen

blocks.note: LI is 51 in Roman numerals
L is the abbreviation for left
Y is the short form of yen, the Japanese currency

explanation.surface: A woman of fifty-one left with only a small amount of Japanese money.
explanation.definitionFit: Lily is a woman's first name, and crosswords often define a given name simply as a woman.

clue.text: Vanity and bile will spread round of necessity

indicators.note: letters that are spread around end up scattered into a different arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Pride and bitterness, the clue warns, are bound to spread.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens of necessity cannot be avoided, which is what inevitably means.

clue.text: Traveller making several round trips?

blocks.note: surface reading: a commuter who makes a number of return journeys
setter's reading: trips round the world, made by someone who tours the planet often

explanation.walkthrough: A round trip normally means there and back; here it means a journey round the globe.
explanation.definitionFit: A globetrotter is a person who travels widely and frequently around the world.

clue.text: Foul 'health town' not so bad on the outside

indicators.note: a piece on the outside wraps around the other piece

blocks.note: better is the comparative of good, so not so bad
a spa is a town people visit to take the healing waters

explanation.surface: A dirty spa town is less unpleasant from the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: Foul reads as an adjective; it is the verb to dirty.
explanation.definitionFit: To bespatter is to splash with mud or dirt, which is a way of fouling something.

clue.text: Ask for meal without starter? Starter wanted!

indicators.note: without its starter means losing the first letter

blocks.note: to beg is to ask for
dinner is a meal

explanation.surface: A diner asks to skip the first course, while a restaurant advertises for an apprentice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' first means the opening letter, then a person starting out.
explanation.definitionFit: A beginner is a novice or someone just starting out, so a starter in that sense.

clue.text: Decide Thames could do for a house

indicators.note: 'do' in the sense of fix up or redo, so the letters get reworked

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Choosing a riverside location for a home on the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi-detached is a British house type joined to one neighbour by a shared wall, so it is a kind of house.

clue.text: Being in state of gloom, old revolutionary skulked

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: to be in a mood is to be sulky
Che Guevara, the Argentine-born revolutionary who died in 1967

explanation.surface: A former revolutionary, depressed, hid away and sulked.
explanation.definitionFit: To mooch is British slang for to loiter or slope about aimlessly, close to skulking.

clue.text: A shirt spoilt — hide new stain

indicators.note: a spoilt item has been messed up, so its letters are jumbled
to hide something is to conceal it inside, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A ruined shirt, and an attempt to cover a fresh mark on it.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarnish is to discolour or blemish, so as a verb it means to stain.

clue.text: Telephone everyone entering the competition

indicators.note: something entering another thing goes inside it

blocks.note: a cup is a knockout competition, such as the FA Cup
all means everyone

explanation.surface: Ringing round so that everybody signs up for the contest.
explanation.definitionFit: To call up is to phone someone, so the phrasal verb matches telephone used as a verb.

clue.text: Man a data recorder, we hear? That could be right

definitions.text: Man a data recorder, we hear? That could be right

indicators.note: what we hear is speech, so the words before are taken by their sound, not their spelling

blocks.note: cat is jazz slang for a man, and a logger is a device that records data

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to staff a recording device, and agrees this might be the correct move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That could be right' nods at the whole clue: said aloud the phrase gives the word, and the word's meaning is a person who records data in lists.
explanation.definitionFit: A cataloguer compiles systematic lists of items, so such a person is literally a man who records data.

clue.text: A product of apples? No hesitation — tart!

indicators.note: a hesitation is the sound of faltering speech, and 'no' removes that sound

blocks.note: taken as written
cider is the drink made from fermented apples
er is the sound of a speaker hesitating

explanation.surface: Something made from apples, served up promptly: a tart.
explanation.walkthrough: The apple tart picture is the trap: 'tart' is the adjective sour, not a pie.
explanation.definitionFit: Acid and tart both describe a sharp, sour taste, so the two adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Book in the end left uncompleted

indicators.note: left unfinished means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: at last means in the end

explanation.surface: A book that was never finished.
explanation.definitionFit: An atlas is a bound volume of maps, so it is a kind of book.

clue.text: Seize some eggs

blocks.note: first meaning: to grab hold of tightly
second meaning: a set of eggs laid together by a bird

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a raid on a henhouse; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means grab tightly, and the noun is the batch of eggs a hen lays and sits on at one time.

clue.text: Wasting medicine that Carol should swallow

indicators.note: whatever swallows something takes it inside, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: to carol is to sing joyfully
a pill is a dose of medicine

explanation.surface: A wasting illness, and the drug a patient named Carol ought to take.
explanation.walkthrough: Carol looks like a woman's name, but it is the verb sing.
explanation.definitionFit: Spilling milk or water wastes it, so spilling can stand for wasting in the sense of letting something go to waste.

clue.text: Heavenly place? Not island in March

indicators.note: 'not' tells the solver to leave out the following abbreviation

blocks.note: paradise is heaven
Is is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A heavenly spot, but no island in the month of March.
explanation.walkthrough: March looks like the month because it opens a word in capitals; it is the verb, to walk in step.
explanation.definitionFit: To parade is to march in a procession, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Prince and his mother briefly providing the drink

blocks.note: Chas is short for Charles, long the Prince of Wales
ER, Elizabeth Regina, was Charles's mother the Queen

explanation.surface: A royal and his mother supplying the drinks at a function.
explanation.walkthrough: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen Elizabeth II, whose son Charles was prince for decades.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaser is a drink taken straight after another, such as a beer after a whisky.
